# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-12 12:22 UTC by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 334 active entries of tips_notebook.json (71 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier sheets are in history/.

## Everyone
- Keep a notepad of each player's stated vote on every nomination and trial, the announced totals and your own vote. Ballots are secret, so a stated vote the totals contradict is a lead to question (usually a miscast), not a hang by itself. (seen in 14 games)
- Totals can be manipulated: a Ballot Stuffer adds a trial vote and a Fixer silently flips one player's. When a total doesn't fit, first ask voters to re-check their reminders; nomination counts can't be altered, so they are the cleaner liar test. (seen in 6 games)
- Spend one-shot tokens the first time they can change a vote or remove a threat; dying with them is the common waste. Kill tokens need a lead first (not a bare claim clash: duplicate claimants are often both real), but fire by parity. (seen in 15 games)
- A visit shows a destination, not an action. A corroborated lone unexplained visitor to a Katana victim is still near-proof; an uncorroborated report is only the claimant's word. (seen in 39 games)
- Each Day, put past results and tonight's plan in your will. The result of the night you die never reaches it, so post what matters publicly. (seen in 39 games)
- Keep votes matching your stated reads and answer direct questions about your night in one plain sentence; evasion tends to become the case against you. (seen in 36 games)
- Check the rules before calling a contradiction: only Smuggler and Vulture are unique, a role-block explains a missing result, and a swap explains an odd one. (seen in 38 games)

## Village
- Hunt Neutral killers on purpose: read every cause of death (a Serial Killer or ignite cause proves one alive), and Not Evil doesn't clear them. Press unwatched Vanilla claimants and unexplained attack survivors, but don't spend hangs on roles that never block wins, and near the vote lock hang the Yakuza lead first. (seen in 10 games)
- Investigators: post target and exact result once it bears on a vote, because held-back results look retrofitted. It rarely pays to announce tonight's target or hint at a power role with no result: that draws the block, the Katana or a Ritualist guess. (seen in 40 games)
- Convict on mechanical cases (a broken claim, a Yakuza-only role claim, an attack slip, elimination from a corroborated result) rather than leans or wording. When no result is coming, the best lead available, such as a pair who PM daily and vote alike, is your case. (seen in 54 games)
- Count the vote lock each morning: once Yakuza hold half the living players, no nomination passes. 'Wait for tonight's results' is often a Yakuza line, and the Day before the lock is the last real hang. (seen in 14 games)
- Once a mechanical result shows someone is Yakuza, those who defended them, argued for delay or PM'd them are the next leads. (seen in 40 games)
- A player who self-nominates, pushes without evidence or reads Evil while asking for the rope is often a Jester. Usually leave them alive; if you hang, keep Guilty to a bare majority, since revenge kills a Guilty voter. (seen in 21 games)
- Survival confirms nothing: ask a Katana survivor to name a protector. Unexplained survival plus Not Evil fits a Serial Killer, and the Katana holder also reads Not Evil. (seen in 24 games)

## Yakuza
- Defending a doomed teammate usually costs more than it saves. Do the vote math in night chat; unless your votes can stop the hang, vote Guilty and say so. (seen in 50 games)
- Plan in night chat, not daytime PMs: everyone sees who messaged whom, and a PM pair often becomes the town's main lead. (seen in 51 games)
- Confirm holder and target every night and have everyone submit the vote; with two Yakuza, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 34 games)
- Agree Village covers before Day 2 that fit your tokens and real visits. Naming a Yakuza-only role is a confession, and switching claims once cornered is usually fatal. (seen in 27 games)
- Kill players whose future results narrow you (Census Taker, Oracle, Cartographer, blockers); near parity, a Vigilante or Sniper with shots comes first. (seen in 23 games)
- After a failed Katana, remove the protector rather than retry. If nobody claims the save, the survivor likely has innate Defense: hang a Serial Killer or Arsonist, because the Katana can't kill them. (seen in 29 games)

## Coroner
- Examine the body that settles a live question (a duplicate claimant, a hanged suspect) on the first night it exists and post the role next Day. Announcing your next exam invites the kill, and a cleaned body yields nothing. (seen in 4 games)

## Medic
- Free Standard protection on claimed investigators stops the Katana but not Strong attacks; spend a token on Strong once a Neutral killer shows. Staying unclaimed tends to avoid blocks. (seen in 31 games)

## Smuggler
- Don't veto swaps for fear of redirecting your own kill: a swap moves exactly the actions aimed at the two swapped players. Aim the Katana at a decoy swapped with the Medic's likely ward, or swap yourself with a Villager to dodge a check, and tell teammates, since their actions move too. (seen in 3 games)

rules:
=== PART 1: THE GAME ===

R1 (Overview and winning)
You are playing a Mafia-style game with around 10 players (depending on setup), each in a faction. An omniscient
moderator runs the game. The game alternates Day and Night phases, starting with Day 1. Day 1 is for talking only:
there are no nominations or trials, and it is shorter than later Days (R16).
- For most roles, you win iff your faction wins. A faction typically wins iff it has players alive at the end.
- The game ends as soon as all living players, ignoring roles that never block wins, belong to one faction. This is
  checked after every death; deaths that happen together at night are checked together.
- Some Neutral roles never block another faction's win (their role says so); their own wins don't depend on how
  the game ends.

R2 (Factions)
- Village (Good): the largest faction, but with weaker roles and less information.
- Yakuza (Evil): fewer players, stronger roles; they know each other and share a night chat.
- Neutral: each Neutral player is their own one-person faction, even if two players have the same Neutral role.
The list of roles in the game is not public. A role may appear more than once in a game, except these unique
roles, which appear at most once: Smuggler, Vulture.

R15 (Alignments)
Every player has one of three alignments: Good (Village), Evil (Yakuza) or Neutral. Some roles and effects change
how a player's alignment appears; see R19.

R18 (Terms)
- Living players: players who haven't died or left. Every count in these rules ("majority", "random player")
  means living players unless it says otherwise.
- Majority: strictly more than half; exactly half is not a majority.
- Action: anything a role does at night by choice or by its rules (investigating, shooting, blocking, ...).
- Visit: an action on another player counts as A visiting B, unless it is an Astral Visit (R6).
- Astral Visit: an action that is not a visit. Abilities that react to visits (Tracker, Lookout,
  Fortune Teller) never see or react to it.
- Alignment check: a result that reports alignment (Sheriff, Seer). See R19 for what they see.
- Exact-role check: a result that reports or tests an exact role (Oracle, Diviner, Ritualist, Mortician, Coroner,
  Talent Agent, a Vigilante's kill).
- Token: a limited-use resource a role starts with. Spent tokens are gone; a role-blocked action spends none.

R11 (The circle)
Players sit in a circle. The dead (and players who leave) are removed from it.

=== PART 2: THE DAY ===

R4 (Day phase, chat, nominations and trials)
Chat:
- There is a public chat and private chats between exactly two players.
- Private messages are not secret: whenever A sends B a private message, everyone sees that A sent B a private
  message, but only A and B see its contents.
Nominations:
- Any player may publicly nominate someone, including themself. All chat stops at once.
- Everyone votes Yes/No at the same time; nobody sees another vote before casting their own. The nominator votes
  Yes by default. There are no abstentions: a player who doesn't vote counts as voting No. Votes are secret: once
  all votes are in, only the number of Yes votes is announced (the nominator is named), never who voted which way.
  Each voter is privately reminded of their own vote.
- If a majority of all votes counted are Yes, the nominee goes on trial.
Trials:
- The nominee says the first public message and may defend themself; others may chat publicly and privately.
  After everyone else has had a turn, the nominee gets one last public message before the vote.
- Then everyone votes Guilty/Innocent at the same time (no abstentions: a player who doesn't vote counts as voting
  Innocent). Votes are secret: only the Guilty and Innocent totals are announced, never who voted which way. Each
  voter is privately reminded of their own vote.
- If a majority of all votes counted are Guilty, the nominee is Executed by Hanging, a Divine Attack, and the Day
  ends immediately.
- If three nominations pass (failed ones don't count) and all three trials end Innocent, the Day ends.
- Some roles can change how votes are counted. If an announced vote total doesn't match the number of voters,
  a role manipulated the count on purpose; it is not an error. One use of such a role can change every trial
  that Day, so the number of changed totals doesn't show how many times a role was used.
Voting Yes or Guilty on yourself is allowed.

R16 (Day length)
Day chat goes around the circle in turns. Each Day the program picks a random living player to speak first;
turns then go around the circle from them in the same order every round. Besides the endings in R4, the Day ends when a full round passes in
which nobody sends a public message or nominates, except that anyone sent a private message during that round
first gets one last turn. The Day also ends after at most 8 rounds (2 on Day 1).

R22 (Speaking budget)
Day messages and nominations cost speaking budget. Each player earns budget every round of a Day, up to a cap, and
part of what they have left carries into the next Day (nothing carries over from Day 1). A message's price grows
with its length and, after the first rounds of a Day, with the round; private messages cost less than public ones.
A nomination costs budget too. On a trial turn prices are lower and each speaker also gets a trial-only budget,
spent first and lost when the turn ends; the accused's first defense message is free up to a set length. The
program sets the numbers for each game and tells every player at the start.

R23 (Swaps)
Some roles can swap two players for a night. Every action that night aimed at one of them, whether or not it visits
(including the Katana's attack, Astral checks such as the Juror's and automatic actions such as the Ex-Con's visit
or the Seer's pair) lands on the other instead, as if its user had chosen that player. Only the swap itself is not
moved (the swapping player's Katana vote is). Results name the player the action's user chose, so a swapped action's
result doesn't show the swap: a Sheriff who checked A learns B's alignment as A's. A result that lists several
players (e.g. a group around the target) is built around B, but A and B trade places in the list, each named where
the other would be; the roles, alignments and counts in it are still the real players', so the rest of the group can
still hint at the swap. A Lookout who watched A watches B instead, and a Tracker sees the player its target's action
landed on. An effect that lasts into the next Day (e.g. listening in on private messages) follows B, and its user is
told at dawn that a swap moved it to B. Effects that pick their own victim at random (e.g. the Jester's revenge or
a Cursed player's curse, R24) aren't actions aimed at a player, so a swap doesn't move them: they hit whoever they draw.

R13 (Last wills)
Players may write and update a last will at the start of each Night, when they choose their night action
(everyone is asked, even with no action), at the beginning of each Day from Day 2 on (except those who died the
night before) and during any of their own Day turns, including on Day 1. Results that arrive later in a
night can't be added that night. When a player dies, their last will is shared publicly at once.

R25 (Day actions)
Some roles act during the Day. A day action is taken on one of your own speaking turns, along with your messages;
not on a trial turn, and not while you are puppeted. It takes effect after a random delay: anywhere from right
after that turn to n-1 speaking turns later, n being the number of players alive when it was taken, every delay
equally likely. Only Day speaking turns count, not trial turns; a turn that starts a trial ends with that trial. So
its timing doesn't show whose turn it was. If the Day ends first, it takes effect as the Day ends. If you died since
taking it, it doesn't take effect. Day actions due at the same time take effect one at a time. A death it causes is
announced at once (R12), and the game ends if that leaves one faction (R1). A day action isn't a visit, and night
protections don't last into the Day.

=== PART 3: THE NIGHT ===

R5 (Night phase)
Chat is off for most players; some (usually a faction, like the Yakuza) have a private night chat. The moderator
wakes players one by one, or faction by faction, to act. When the Night ends, the moderator works out every
effect. By default, effects are announced publicly at the start of the next Day; some are not announced.

R7 (Optional actions)
Every ability is optional ("may") unless its role says "must": any player may choose not to act at Night, not to
use a Day ability, and not to spend a token. Effects a role has automatically, with no choice (e.g. the
Ex-Con's nightly visit), aren't optional, but a role-block still stops them (R9).

R6 (Visits)
- When A performs an action on B, A visits B, unless the action is an Astral Visit.
- A role that targets a player may target itself unless its text says otherwise (e.g. "other than yourself").
- A player whose role can target others but who targets themself shows as visiting themself.
- A player whose action can only affect themself does not show as visiting anyone.
- An action that targets no player (e.g. the Clerk's rig) is not a visit.
- A player who visits the same target with several actions in one night is one visitor to that target: anything
  that lists, counts or reacts to visitors (a watch, a Veteran's alert) treats them once.

R9 (Role-blocks)
A role-blocked player's actions that night have no effect, exactly as if they had chosen not to act: no visit,
no tokens spent. It lasts only that one night (not the next Day or later nights). Role-blocked players are told
they were role-blocked. Any player can be role-blocked unless their role says otherwise; blocking a player who
has no night action, or who chose not to act, has no other effect, but they are still told. A role-blocker learns
only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked.
A result a role gets with no action at all (its text says "This needs no action") isn't an action, so a role-block
doesn't stop it; automatic actions, such as the Ex-Con's visit or the Seer's random pair, are stopped (R7).

R10 (Simultaneous night resolution)
All night actions happen at the same time. Think of it as two steps: first everyone attempts their actions,
then all results happen together. So investigations that give their result at the end of the night (e.g. the
Seer's random pair) draw from and report on everyone alive when the night began, including players who die that
night.

R21 (Effects that outlast their user)
An effect set up at night for the following Day (e.g. a Clerk's rig, a Prosecutor's prosecution) still happens if
its user dies that night, unless it needs its user to act during that Day (e.g. a Puppeteer writing the puppet's
messages, a Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote); those lapse. Any token spent on it is gone either way (R18).

R20 (Night resolution checklist): a summary of the rules above, in the order the moderator applies them.
1. Remove actions of role-blocked players (R9), automatic ones included (the Ex-Con's visit, the Seer's pair).
   Party Animal, Pharmacist, Smuggler and Veteran can't be role-blocked. Swaps (R23) apply before anything else.
2. Work out who visits whom (R6), including the Katana holder's visit (R8) and the Ex-Con's random visit.
3. Attacks: each kills iff its level beats the target's Defense (R3). Defenses don't stack; the highest counts.
   A trap stops one attack before Defense and may hit its attacker back (Trapper).
4. Results for investigators, using the visits and appearances (R19).
5. Notifications: attackers learn whether they succeeded, attacked players learn the attacking role (R3, with the
   Katana exception in R8), protectors learn nothing (R17), role-blocked players are told (R9), Yakuza learn each
   other's actions (R8).
6. Deaths are revealed at the start of the Day (R12); the win check runs on all of the night's deaths together (R1).

=== PART 4: ATTACKS, DEATH AND INFORMATION ===

R3 (Attack and Defense)
- Levels, lowest to highest: None, Basic, Standard, Strong, Divine. Players have Defense None by default.
- An Attack kills iff its level is strictly higher than the target's Defense.
- Defenses don't stack: a player with several sources of Defense has the highest of them.
- By default the attacker learns whether the Attack succeeded (not the target's Defense), and the target learns
  the role that attacked them (not the attacker's name or Attack level). A target hit by several Attacks in one
  night learns the role behind each, including those that failed. The Katana is an exception (R8).

R17 (Protection feedback)
Protectors (e.g. the Medic) are never told whether their protection stopped an attack, and a protected player is
never told who protected them. A player who is attacked is still told as in R3.

R12 (Death reveals)
When someone dies, their cause of death (e.g. Katana, Vigilante, Execution by Hanging) and last will are revealed
publicly; their role and alignment are not. If several attacks were each fatal, every fatal cause is revealed;
attacks the player survived aren't. The dead leave the circle and can't take part in the game any more. A player
whose win ends their part in the game (a hanged Jester, an Executioner who leaves) is the exception: the
announcement of their win names their role.

R14 (Stall rule)
If a Day begins and nobody has died in the three previous Nights and three previous Days, everyone loses. Deaths
from last Night count even though they're announced today. Every death counts; leaving (like the Executioner's)
doesn't.

R19 (What investigations see)
Alignment checks (Sheriff: Evil / Not Evil; Seer: compares Good / Neutral / Evil) see a player's true alignment,
except:
- Yakuza holding the Katana at the end of the night: Good (Sheriff: Not Evil), even if they died that night.
- Player framed by the Fabricator that night: Evil.
- Ex-Con, and a player with the Notorious trait (R24): Evil.
- Sheriff on Neutrals: Jester and Executioner read Evil; Serial Killer and Arsonist read Not Evil. (Seers see
  every Neutral as Neutral.)
The Census Taker's count is not an alignment check: it always sees true alignment, so none of the exceptions
above apply to it.
Exact-role checks see the true role. The Roleplayer is seen as "Roleplayer".
Token counts (Accountant) see the true total at the end of the night. The Roleplayer is seen as having 0 tokens,
even though they believe they have their fake role's tokens.
Visit-based results (Tracker, Lookout, Fortune Teller, Cartographer, Scout) are never changed by any of these.

R24 (Traits)
Some players also have a trait: an extra ability on top of their role. You are told your own trait at the start;
nobody else is told, not even your teammates, and whether a game has any traits is secret. Investigations never see
traits: they report roles and alignments only. A trait stays with you if your role changes. Traits are always true:
a Roleplayer's trait is real even though its role isn't. A player may have more than one trait, but never the same
one twice. Each trait says which players can get it. A trait's night action is used in addition to your role's own,
and a role-block stops it too.
- Martyr (Village players only): if you are hanged, the announcement of your death also says you were a Martyr and
  names every player whose vote counted as Guilty in your trial. Your role stays hidden. A Martyr who dies any
  other way shows nothing.
- Armed (Village players only): once per game, at night, you may fire a hidden gun at another living player: a
  Basic Attack. It is an action and a visit, and a role-blocked shot isn't used up. You learn only whether it
  killed its target. A kill's cause is "a hidden gun".
- Cursed (Village players only): if you die, a random living Good player (if any) is dealt a Divine Attack at the
  end of the night: the night you died, or the night after the Day you died. It comes after all of that night's
  other actions and attacks, so the victim is drawn from the Good players still alive then, and it counts as a
  death that night. Its cause is "a curse". It needs no action, so a role-block doesn't stop it.
- Avenger (Village players only): if you are killed at night, every player whose attack would have killed you is
  dealt a Divine Attack and dies too, with the cause "Avenger". Attacks that weren't fatal on their own, and deaths
  by Day, set nothing off. It needs no action, so a role-block doesn't stop it.
- Kindred (Village players only): after each trial vote you cast, you privately learn up to two random other
  players whose votes counted the same way as the vote you cast (if fewer did, you learn that). It needs no action,
  so a role-block doesn't stop it.
- Faultline (Village players only): after each trial vote you cast, you privately learn one random other player
  whose vote counted as Guilty and one whose vote counted as Innocent (if all the others voted one way, you learn
  that). It needs no action, so a role-block doesn't stop it.
- Notorious (Village players only): alignment checks see you as Evil (R19), like the Ex-Con. Checks that see
  true alignment, such as the Census Taker's count, aren't fooled.
- Grudge (any player): if you are hanged, the next night one random player whose vote counted as Guilty in your
  trial, among those alive when that night begins, is dealt a Standard Attack (an Astral Visit). Defense and
  protection apply as usual. A kill's cause is "a grudge". It needs no action, so a role-block doesn't stop it.
- Loud (any player): you earn 1.5 times the usual speaking budget each round, and your cap is 1.5 times the usual
  (R22). Your prices and trial-only budget are the usual ones.
- Curt (any player): the length part of your message prices (R22) is doubled, so long messages cost you much more;
  each message's base fee, nominations and your trial-only budget are the usual ones.
- Confidant (any player): once per game, on one of your own Day turns (not while puppeted), you may send one
  private message hidden: nobody else is told it was sent, and the public ledger doesn't count it. Its recipient
  sees that it was hidden. Players who hear private messages (e.g. the Wiretap) still hear it, also marked hidden.

=== PART 5: THE YAKUZA ===

R8 (Yakuza and the Katana)
- One random Yakuza starts with the Katana. The Yakuza share a private chat at night.
- Each night the Yakuza vote, at the same time, on who holds the Katana that night (and the next Day) and whom it
  attacks, if anyone. Both choices need a majority of living Yakuza; with two Yakuza alive, both must agree.
  Without a majority on a target, no attack happens; without a majority on a holder, the Katana doesn't move.
  A majority may move the Katana without attacking.
- The Katana attack is Standard and is dealt by whoever holds it at the end of the night. It is an action and a
  visit by that player (the new holder, if it moved that night): role-blocking them stops it, and Trackers see
  them visit the target. Moving or passing the Katana isn't an action: a role-block doesn't stop it (a blocked
  new holder still gets the Katana, but their attack fails), and it isn't a visit.
- The holder may also use their own role's night action.
- The holder appears Good to alignment checks that night (R19).
- The attacked player only learns they were attacked with the Katana, not the Yakuza role.
- At the end of the night, each Yakuza learns what actions the other Yakuza chose, but not their results
  (e.g. whether the Pharmacist's block worked) or whether a teammate was role-blocked.
- Role-blocked Yakuza still vote on the Katana's holder and target; the votes aren't actions.
- If the holder dies, the Katana passes to a random living Yakuza, if any; a holder who dies at night passes it on
  after that night's results. The living Yakuza are told who holds it now (and so learn that the holder died).

=== PART 6: ROLES ===

Every role lists the same fields. Defaults, unless a role says otherwise: Defense None, no tokens, appears as its
true alignment (R19), night action is a visit.

--- Village (Good) ---

Townsfolk (most villagers, helpful to the Village)

Vanilla Villager
  Night: none.

Investigative

Sheriff
  Night: may investigate one player. Learn Evil or Not Evil (alignment check, R19).

Tracker
  Night: may track one player. Learn whom they visited.

Lookout
  Night: may watch one player. Learn who visited them, not counting your own visit.

Seer
  Tokens: 1 seer token.
  Night: at the end of every night, you are told two random players other than yourself who were alive when the
  night began (players who die that night count, R10), and whether their alignments (Good/Neutral/Evil) are the
  same (alignment check, R19). Instead, you may spend a token to choose the
  two living players yourself (not including yourself). A chosen pair is a visit to both players; the random
  pair isn't a visit. A role-block stops both.

Fortune Teller
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn two numbers about that night, each labeled: how many players were
  visited (a player visited several times counts once), and how many players visited anyone (a player who visited
  several players counts once). This needs no action. Self-visits (R6) count in both numbers.
  Example: A holds the Katana, attacks B and also uses their own role's action on C, D visits B, and E protects
  themself. Visited: B, C and E, so 3. Visitors: A, D and E, so 3. Equal numbers don't mean nobody was visited
  twice.

Oracle
  Night: may guess one player's exact role (Astral Visit). At the end of the night, learn whether you were right.

Eavesdropper
  Night: may eavesdrop on one player. Only during the following Day (not the Night you eavesdrop), you read the contents of every private
  message they send or receive, as it is sent. Puppeted messages reach you as the puppet's (you aren't told about
  the puppeting). They aren't told.

Archivist
  Tokens: 1 archive token.
  Night: may spend the token to consult the archive. At the end of the night, let N be the number of players other
  than you who were alive when the night began (players who died that night count): you are shown N roles, in
  random order and without names, of which floor(0.5 * N) are real and the rest are fake. The real ones are the
  roles of floor(0.5 * N) of those players, chosen at random; a role appears as many times as it was drawn, so
  two drawn Vanilla Villagers show twice. This is an exact-role check (R19).
  Each fake is drawn at random from all the roles in these rules, including roles that are in the game, except
  that the result never shows a unique role (R2) twice.

Surveyor
  Tokens: 3 survey tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to survey one player other than yourself. The group is that player plus their nearest
  neighbor on each side in the circle (R11) among the players alive at the start of the night, skipping yourself
  and never counting anyone twice (so with only one or two other players alive, the group is smaller). You are
  told who was in the group and the exact role of one of them chosen at random, but not whose it is. Players who
  die that night can still be chosen. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Census Taker
  Night: may take a census around one player other than yourself (a visit to that player only).
  The program adds two other players drawn at random from everyone alive at the start of the night except you
  (players who die that night can be drawn; if fewer than two others are left, the group is smaller). It also
  draws at random whether to count Good or Evil players. You are told who was in the group, which alignment was
  counted, and how many of the group are of it. It counts true alignment and is not an alignment check (R19):
  the Katana holder, framed players and the Ex-Con count as what they really are, and
  Outsiders (e.g. the Roleplayer and the Ex-Con) count as Good. Neutral players are never
  counted, as either Good or Evil.

Coroner
  Tokens: 3 coroner tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to examine one player who died before the night began (not one who left the game, and not
  one who dies tonight). You learn their role, unless a Mortician cleaned them: then you learn only that. This is an
  Astral Visit (R6) and an exact-role check (R19).

Chronicler
  Tokens: 2 chronicler tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to mark one player other than yourself. This is a visit. The marked player isn't told.
  The mark lasts for the rest of the game, even after you die. If a marked player dies, at any time and of any
  cause, the announcement of their death also reveals their true role to everyone (an exact-role check, R19), and
  says they had been marked by a Chronicler (not by whom). A Mortician's clean beats the mark: a marked player who
  is cleaned has their role and will hidden, and the announcement says they had been marked but the clean hid their
  role. You can't mark a player you already marked. Marking a player another Chronicler already marked spends your
  token but adds nothing.

Auditor
  Night: may audit one player other than yourself. You learn every vote they cast during the Day just before this
  Night, in order: Yes or No on each nomination and Guilty or Innocent in each trial. If they cast none, you learn
  that. A doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) shows as a single Guilty or Innocent.

Juror
  Night: may name two different players other than yourself (dead players allowed; Astral Visit). You learn how many
  times they voted the same way, over every Day so far, counted separately for trial votes (Guilty/Innocent) and
  nomination votes (Yes/No), e.g. "the same way in 3 of 4 trial votes and 5 of 9 nomination votes". Only votes
  both of them cast count, and not votes on the nomination or trial of either of them. A doubled vote (Ballot
  Stuffer) counts once. You learn only the totals, not which votes they agreed on.

Bloodhound
  Tokens: 2 scent tokens.
  Night: at the end of every night, code draws three random players other than you from those alive at the start of
  the night, and you learn their names and one combined count: how many Attacks (R3) the three have made in total
  this game, tonight's included, whether or not the Attacks killed anyone. Each player's Katana attacks, shots,
  alert or trap hits and so on all count; a role-blocked attack never happened, so it doesn't. This needs no action
  and a role-block doesn't stop it.
  Night: may also spend a token to track one player other than yourself: they take one of the three places that
  night and code draws the other two. A role-block stops the tracking (R9) but not the result.

Scrutineer
  Night: may scrutinize one player other than yourself who voted in the Day's trials (Astral Visit). Code adds two
  random other players who voted in those trials (never you), and you learn the three names and, for each trial of
  the Day just before this Night, how many of the three voted Guilty, e.g. "2 in the trial of Erin; 0 in the trial
  of Frank". You don't learn which of them voted which way. A doubled vote (Ballot Stuffer) counts once. If there
  was no trial that Day, you learn that.

Profiler
  Tokens: 3 profile tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to profile one player other than yourself. You learn three different roles, exactly one
  of which is that player's true role. Of the other two, one is drawn at random from the roles of the other players
  alive at the start of the night (including players who die that night, but not yourself), and the other from the
  roles that no player in the game has. At least one of the three is a Good role and at least one is not Good (Evil
  or Neutral), so a result never settles the player's alignment on its own; which of the two supplies the missing
  side is random. When no role fits a draw, that one is drawn from all roles in these rules instead. The three are
  different and listed in alphabetical order. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Cartographer
  Tokens: 2 map tokens.
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn the sizes of that night's visit groups. Link two players whenever one
  visited the other that night (R6). Direction is ignored: A visiting B links them exactly as B visiting A
  would. A group is a set of players linked to each other, directly or through other players. Every player alive at
  the start of the night (including players who die that night) is in exactly one group, so a player who visited no
  one and was visited by no one is a group of 1, and a self-visit links no one. You learn only the sizes, largest
  first (e.g. "4, 2, 1, 1, 1"). This needs no action and a role-block doesn't stop it.
  Night: may also spend a token to map one player (Astral Visit; yourself allowed): at the end of the night you also
  learn the names of everyone in that player's group. A role-block stops the map (R9) but not the sizes.
  Your own actions never visit anyone, so they never link you to anyone.

Scout
  Night: at the end of every night, you learn the names of three players (you may be one of them) who were each in a
  different visit group that night. Groups are as for the Cartographer (visit direction is ignored). The names are
  drawn like this: a random player, then a random player outside the groups already drawn from, and so on, so a big
  group is more likely to come up than a small one. If there were fewer than three groups, you learn one name per
  group and how many groups there were. This needs no action and a role-block doesn't stop it. You never visit
  anyone.

Insomniac
  Tokens: 2 insomniac tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to stay awake. At the end of the night, you learn the roles of up to 3 players who visited
  someone that night (R6; a visit to themselves counts), but not who they are: if more than 3 players visited, 3 of
  them are drawn at random. The roles are listed in alphabetical order, and a role shows twice if two of those
  players have it. If fewer than 3 players visited, you learn all of their roles, and if nobody visited, you learn
  that. Players who visited and then died that night count. Only visits count: an action that isn't a visit (e.g.
  an Astral Visit or a Veteran's alert) doesn't. Staying awake is not a visit. This is an exact-role check (R19).

Accountant
  Night: may audit one player. Learn how many tokens they have in total at the end of the night, after any they
  spent that night and any a Magpie stole (token count, R19). You learn only the total, not what kind of tokens
  they are.
  If their role changed at the end of this night, the role just before the change counts.

Protective

Medic
  Tokens: 2 medic tokens.
  Night: may protect one player other than yourself, giving them Standard Defense. Spend 1 token to give Strong
  Defense instead, and 1 token to protect yourself instead of another player; the two can be combined (so
  protecting yourself costs 1 token with Standard Defense and 2 with Strong).

Trapper
  Night: may place a trap on one player other than yourself and other than the player your trap is already on, or
  may remove your trap (removing it isn't a visit). You have one trap at a time; a new trap replaces the old one at
  once. Traps last even after you die. A trap is armed from the next night on: the first time anyone makes a Basic,
  Standard or Strong Attack on the trapped player on a later night, the trap is used up and stops that attack
  (chosen at random if there are several; Divine Attacks ignore it); any other attacks resolve as usual. The trap
  acts before Defense, after any protection that acts before all others. If the stopped attack was a visit, its
  attacker is dealt a Strong Attack, whatever their faction; an Astral attack is stopped without one. You learn
  that your trap went off, and nothing else (not whose attack, nor whether the trap killed).

Kitsune
  Tokens: 1 kitsune token.
  Night: if you hold no swallowed attack, may lay a fox charm on one player other than yourself (on yourself, spend
  the token). The charm acts before any other protection: it swallows one Basic, Standard or Strong Attack on that
  player tonight (chosen at random if there are several; Divine Attacks ignore it), which then has no effect (its
  attacker and target are told as for any failed attack, R3); any other attacks on them resolve as usual. Several
  charms on one player act one at a time, in random order, each swallowing a different attack. You keep the
  swallowed attack and learn its level and how its kill would be announced. While you hold it you can't lay a charm:
  on a night you choose a target, you release it on that player (not yourself), as an Attack of the same level whose
  kill is announced with the same cause (a released Katana attack reads as a Katana death), and a survivor is told
  it came from that cause's role. You keep the attack until you release it, and it's lost if you die. You learn
  whether your charm swallowed an attack, and whether your release killed.

Killing

Vigilante
  Tokens: 3 vigilante tokens.
  Night: may shoot one player: 1 token for a Basic Attack, 2 for Standard, 3 for Strong. If your shot kills them,
  you also learn their role (exact-role check, R19).

Enforcer
  Tokens: 3 enforcer tokens.
  Night: may visit one player other than yourself. If they made an Attack of their own choosing tonight (fatal or
  not; a Katana attack counts for its holder; a Veteran's alert, a trap or a revenge doesn't count), you deal them a
  Basic Attack. Spend 1 token to also visit a second player, and 1 token to make your Attack Strong; the two can be
  combined. If both players you visit made an Attack, one of them, chosen at random, is attacked. Tokens are spent
  whether or not you attack. You learn whether you attacked and whether it killed; with one target you know whom,
  with two you aren't told which.

Veteran
  Tokens: 3 alert tokens.
  You can't be role-blocked.
  Night: may spend a token to go on alert (not a visit, R6, so nothing that reacts to visits counts it). While on
  alert you have Standard Defense and you deal a Strong Attack to every player who visits you that night, whatever
  their faction (a role-blocker who visits you is attacked too), however many there are. Astral Visits aren't
  visits, so they aren't attacked. At the end of the night you learn whether anyone visited you and, if so, how
  many, and whether your attack on each of them succeeded, but nothing about who they were.

Sniper
  Tokens: 3 sniper tokens.
  Day: on one of your own speaking turns (once a Day), may take a shot at one player: 1 token for a Basic Attack, 2
  for Standard, 3 for Strong. It is fired after a random delay (R25): everyone is told that someone shot at that
  player, then whether they died; nobody is told who shot. If the target died before then, the shot isn't fired
  and its tokens come back. A Defense from a night effect (e.g. the Medic's) has ended by Day.

Support

Prosecutor
  Tokens: 2 prosecutor tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to prosecute someone. At the start of the next Day, before anyone speaks, the moderator
  announces that someone is being prosecuted; this counts as a successful nomination and they go to trial. It
  counts toward the Day's three-nomination limit, an execution ends the Day as usual, and it can combine with a
  Clerk's rig. If the trial needs a "nominator", the moderator picks a random player.

Party Animal
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Night: may visit one player, role-blocking them.

Philanthropist
  Tokens: 2 philanthropy tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to hand another player one token of their own role's kind (e.g. a medic token to a
  Medic; one kind chosen at random if their role has several). They are told a Philanthropist handed them a token.
  If their role has no tokens, they are told they threw it away because they have no use for it, so it doesn't
  count toward their tokens (e.g. for the Accountant). You are not told which happened.

Outsiders (Village roles: Good, and win with the Village, but the role helps the Village less or can hurt it)

Roleplayer
  You are told your role is X, chosen at random at the start from Sheriff, Tracker, Lookout, Seer, Fortune Teller,
  Oracle and Accountant.
  You aren't told that you're a Roleplayer. The moderator gives you results that are usually false but plausible.
  Exact-role checks see you as Roleplayer (R19). Your night actions only happen in your imagination: they aren't
  visits, have no effect, and no other role sees them.

Ex-Con
  Appears: Evil to alignment checks (R19).
  Night: every night you visit a random player other than yourself, and you aren't told whom. A role-block stops
  the visit (R7).

--- Yakuza (Evil) ---
All Yakuza share the Katana and night chat (R8).

Grunt
  Night: none of its own.

Pharmacist
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Night: may role-block one player.

Ritualist
  Tokens: 2 ritual tokens.
  Night: may guess one player's exact role (Astral Visit), spending 1 token for a Standard Attack or 2 for a
  Divine Attack. If right, the Attack is dealt. If wrong, the moderator publicly announces at the start of the
  next Day that you are a Ritualist. The tokens are spent either way.

Puppeteer
  Tokens: 1 puppet token.
  Night: may spend a token to puppet any player for the following Day (puppeting yourself changes nothing). That
  Day, they are told they are being puppeted, and they can't chat or see private messages; nobody else is told. You
  chat publicly and privately in their place (including seeing their private messages) and can set their claim,
  which appears in the ledger as theirs; that is all you can do for them. They still nominate, vote and so on as
  normal. It lasts one Day.

Fabricator
  Tokens: 1 fabricator token.
  Night: may visit one non-Yakuza player to frame them (no token needed): that night they appear Evil to
  alignment checks (R19); other results are unchanged. On the same visit, you may spend a token to forge that
  player's last will (not anyone else's): if they die of any cause that night, your forged will replaces theirs.
  Framing and forging together are one visit.

Clerk
  Tokens: 1 clerk token.
  Night: may spend a token to rig the next Day's votes. On a rigged Day, anyone successfully nominated is executed.
  The Guilty/Innocent vote still happens; if a majority votes Guilty, the rig is not announced, otherwise it is
  announced publicly.

Smuggler
  Immune to role-blocks.
  Tokens: 2 swap tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to swap two different living players (yourself included) for the night (R23). You visit
  both of them. Both swapped players are told they were swapped, but not with whom.

Ballot Stuffer
  Tokens: 2 ballot tokens.
  Night: may spend a token so that during the following Day your vote counts twice in every Guilty/Innocent trial
  vote. It does not count twice in nomination (Yes/No) votes, which stay one vote each. A trial that Day needs a
  majority of all votes counted, so your extra vote counts whether you vote Guilty or Innocent. The announced
  totals include your extra vote without saying whose it is.

Fixer
  Tokens: 2 fixer tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to fix one player other than yourself. During the following Day, every Guilty/Innocent
  trial vote they cast counts as the opposite (Guilty as Innocent, Innocent as Guilty). Their nomination (Yes/No)
  votes are unchanged. Nobody is told, not even them: their private reminder shows the vote they cast, while the
  totals and anything that reports how they voted (e.g. the Auditor, the Informant, a Jester's revenge on Guilty
  voters) use the vote as counted.

Diviner
  Night: may pick one player. If they are Yakuza, they get Strong Defense for that night. Otherwise, the group is
  that player plus their nearest neighbor on each side in the circle (R11) among the players alive at the start of
  the night, skipping yourself and never counting anyone twice. You are told who was in the group and the exact
  role of one of them (exact-role check, R19), but not whose it is: it is the player you picked with 60% chance,
  otherwise one of the others (20% each, or 40% if there is only one other). Yakuza in the group and players who
  die that night can be drawn too.

Mortician
  Tokens: 3 mortician tokens.
  Night: may spend a token to try to clean someone. If they die that night by any cause, they are cleaned: their
  death is revealed publicly with its cause, but their last will shows as "cleaned by mortician". You are
  privately told their role and last will. A Coroner who examines a cleaned player learns nothing, and a
  cleaned player's role stays hidden even if a Chronicler marked them (the announcement says so). The token is
  spent even if they survive.

Wiretap
  You passively read the contents of every private message sent during the Day, between any two players. This is
  not a night action or a visit, so role-blocks don't stop it. Puppeted messages reach you as the puppet's (you
  aren't told about the puppeting). Nobody is told that a Wiretap exists.

Informant
  You passively see how every player voted in each Guilty/Innocent trial vote, right after the vote. This is not a
  night action or a visit, so role-blocks don't stop it. Nobody is told that an Informant exists, and the other
  Yakuza aren't told the votes: what you share in the night chat is up to you.

Talent Agent
  Tokens: 3 talent tokens, at most one a night.
  Night: may spend a token on one of these (not a visit; it targets no player). "In play" means the true role of a
  player alive when the night began (an exact-role check, R19):
  - Scan: learn one random non-Yakuza role that is in play and one random non-Yakuza role from these rules that
    isn't.
  - Count: name any role in these rules and learn how many players have it in play.

--- Neutral ---
Each Neutral player is their own faction (R2).

Serial Killer
  Defense: Standard. Appears: Not Evil to the Sheriff.
  Win: only alone (not even with another Serial Killer).
  Night: may deal a Strong Attack to one player.

Arsonist
  Defense: Standard. Appears: Not Evil to the Sheriff.
  Win: only alone (not even with another Arsonist).
  Night: may douse one player, or ignite (Astral Visit), dealing a Strong Attack to every doused player. A doused
  player who isn't Good (Yakuza or Neutral) is told at the end of the night that an Arsonist doused them; Good
  players are never told. Igniting uses up every douse: players who survive it are no longer doused.

Jester
  Defense: Basic. Appears: Evil to the Sheriff.
  Never blocks wins (R1).
  Win: iff you are hanged during a Day (other daytime deaths don't count). You lose if the game ends with you
  alive.
  Revenge: if you are hanged, the following night a random Guilty voter from your trial who was alive when that
  night began is dealt a Divine Attack (Astral Visit). If nobody voted Guilty, nothing happens.

Executioner
  Defense: Basic. Appears: Evil to the Sheriff.
  Never blocks wins (R1).
  At the start you get a random target: any player except yourself.
  Win: iff your target is hanged during a Day while you are alive (other daytime deaths don't count). You lose if
  the game ends with your target alive.
  On winning: the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game. Leaving works exactly like dying (you
  leave the circle for good) except it doesn't count as a death. The following night, a random Guilty voter from
  the trial who was alive when that night began (not you, since you left) is dealt a Divine Attack (Astral Visit). If nobody voted
  Guilty, nothing happens.
  If your target dies any other way, or leaves the game, you become a Jester.

Bounty Hunter
  Tokens: 1 attack token. Never blocks wins (R1).
  At the start you get 3 random targets: any players except yourself.
  Night: may spend the token to deal a Strong Attack to one player.
  A bounty on a target is claimed if they die by your attack or are hanged during a Day while your vote counted as
  Guilty. If a target dies any other way (or leaves the game), that bounty is lost. Night deaths are simultaneous
  (R10): a target you kill on the night you die still counts.
  Win: iff you claim 2 bounties. If you are alive then, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game
  (leaving works as for the Executioner). If you have died, you still win and nothing is revealed.
  Lose: once you can no longer claim 2 bounties; if you are alive, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave
  the game.

Magpie
  Defense: Basic. Never blocks wins (R1). Random setups include a Magpie only if at least a third of the roles have tokens.
  Night: may steal a token from another player (a visit). It happens at the end of the night, after that night's
  token use, so a token used tonight can't be stolen. The stolen token is gone (you can't use it). You are told
  whether you stole one, not its kind; they are told which kind they lost. If they have no tokens, nothing
  happens and they aren't told.
  Win: iff you steal tokens from 3 different players (a second steal from the same player takes nothing). If you
  are alive then, the moderator reveals you at once and you leave the game (as for the Executioner). If you died
  that night, you still win and nothing is revealed.

Vulture
  Win: alone, if you are alive at the start of a Day (after the night's deaths) and max(floor(N/4), 2) or fewer
  players are alive, counting yourself, where N is the number of players at the start of the game. The game then
  ends at once and everyone else loses (wins already earned by roles that never block wins still count, R1).
  Night: none.
  Day: at the start of each Day, you learn a role for each player who died since the previous Day began (during that
  Day or the night after it; not players who left the game): with 50% chance it is their true
  role (exact-role check, R19), otherwise it is a different role drawn at random
  from all the roles in these rules. You aren't told which. This isn't an action, so a role-block doesn't stop it.
